_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 7 specification: four sections A–D, ten questions, each section the answer two or three times. Every question paraphrases its section, and several have a near-miss (Gareth disliked his teacher vs Lin who liked hers but not her lessons; Priya's borrowed book vs Joel's gift of tapes; Lin's late understanding vs Gareth's late discovery; Lin's borrowed method vs Priya's borrowed attitude). Used by the Part 7 practice page and by Full test 7.
title: The teacher who changed everything
subtitle: Four adults describe a teacher who made a difference to their lives.

sections.A: Priya, 38, marine biologist. At fourteen I was failing biology and had decided, quite firmly, that science was for other people. Mr Hale, who taught chemistry rather than biology, noticed me drawing crabs in the margin of my exercise book during a detention he was supervising. Instead of telling me off, he asked whether I knew how crabs breathed. I didn't. The next day he left a battered book about seashore life on my desk and said I could give it back whenever I'd finished. I kept it for two years. What I remember most, though, is how he reacted when I got something wrong. He'd say, 'Good, now we know one thing it isn't,' as if a wrong answer had moved us forward. Within a year I was near the top of the class, and I've never been afraid of a failed experiment since.
sections.B: Gareth, 54, carpenter. I'll be honest: for my whole first term I couldn't stand Mrs Lowe. She taught English, she was strict about spelling, and I was a boy who spent every lesson staring out of the window at the school's broken fence. One afternoon she caught me sketching a design for a new one and, to my horror, took the drawing straight to the head teacher. A week later I was building that fence with the caretaker every Wednesday afternoon instead of doing sport. She'd arranged the whole thing. My spelling didn't improve much, but for the first time school felt like a place where I was useful. Years later, at her retirement party, her husband told me she'd grown up on a farm and had once dreamed of being a builder, which nobody at school had ever known. It explained a lot.
sections.C: Lin, 45, hospital manager. Everybody liked Mr Banerjee, me included, but I found his history lessons infuriating. They were mostly arguments. He'd give us two accounts of the same event that completely contradicted each other and refuse to tell us which one was true. At sixteen I wanted facts I could write down and learn for the exam, and I said so, often. It was only in my thirties, sitting in meetings where everyone had a different version of what had gone wrong, that I understood what he'd been preparing us for. Nobody else in the room seemed to know what to do with two stories that didn't match. I now run training days for new managers, and I'll admit I've stolen his approach completely. I hand them two reports of the same incident and wait. They find it just as annoying as I did.
sections.D: Joel, 31, sound engineer. Ms Varga was only at our school for one term, covering for our music teacher, who'd broken her leg skiing. She ignored the lesson plans she'd been left. Instead, she brought in an old tape recorder and sent us round the building to record whatever we could hear: the dinner hall, the bell, rain on the roof of the bike shed. Then she showed us how to cut the sounds up and layer them into a kind of piece. I was a quiet kid who'd never been good at anything in particular, and suddenly I was the one everybody came to for help. On her last day she gave me a box of blank tapes to keep. I've tried for years to find her, through old staff lists and social media, with no luck. If she ever reads this: the bike shed recording still hangs on my studio wall.

questions.question: Which person had a low opinion of the teacher to begin with?
questions.why: 'For my whole first term I couldn't stand Mrs Lowe.' Lin found the lessons infuriating, but she liked Mr Banerjee himself.

questions.question: Which person was allowed to borrow something that belonged to the teacher?
questions.why: Mr Hale left a book on her desk and said she 'could give it back whenever I'd finished'. Joel's tapes were a present 'to keep', not a loan.

questions.question: Which person was taught by someone who was temporarily replacing another member of staff?
questions.why: Ms Varga was there 'for one term, covering for our music teacher'.

questions.question: Which person only saw the point of the teacher's lessons many years afterwards?
questions.why: 'Only in my thirties … I understood what he'd been preparing us for.' Gareth also learned something years later, but it was about Mrs Lowe's past, not the value of her teaching.

questions.question: Which person was doing badly in a subject before the teacher became involved?
questions.why: 'At fourteen I was failing biology.' Gareth's spelling was weak, but he says it 'didn't improve much', so the teacher's effect was elsewhere.

questions.question: Which person has made efforts to contact the teacher again?
questions.why: 'I've tried for years to find her, through old staff lists and social media.' Gareth met his teacher again, but only by going to her retirement party.

questions.question: Which person was given the chance to put a practical ability to use outside lessons?
questions.why: His fence design led to building it 'with the caretaker every Wednesday afternoon instead of doing sport'. Joel's recording happened during music lessons.

questions.question: Which person deliberately uses the teacher's way of teaching in their own job?
questions.why: 'I've stolen his approach completely': she gives new managers two reports of one incident. Priya kept Mr Hale's attitude to mistakes, not his teaching method.

questions.question: Which person had a teacher who treated errors as a kind of progress?
questions.why: 'Good, now we know one thing it isn't': a wrong answer 'had moved us forward'.

questions.question: Which person discovered that the teacher had once had a very different ambition?
questions.why: Her husband revealed she 'had once dreamed of being a builder, which nobody at school had ever known'.
